nodes.name: ambient manifold $M$ of dimension $m$
nodes.statement: Consider a smooth manifold $M$ of dimension $m$.

nodes.name: local reduction to $\mathbb{R}^m$
nodes.statement: For local questions we can take $M=\mathbb{R}^m$, which could correspond to a chart around some point $x_0\in M$.

nodes.name: smoothness convention
nodes.statement: All functions, vector fields and differential forms are presumed to be smooth ($C^\infty$).

nodes.name: involutivity
nodes.statement: Let $L_i = \sum_{k=1}^m f_i^k(x) \partial/\partial x^j$, $i=1,\ldots,r\le m$, be first order differential operators, such that the vector fields $v_i(x) = (f_i^k(x))_{k=1}^m$ are linearly independent. They are said to be in \emph{involution} when there exist functions $c^k_{ij}(x)$ such that \[ L_i L_j - L_j L_i = \sum_{k=1}^r c^k_{ij}(x) L_k . \]
differentia: there exist functions $c^k_{ij}(x)$ such that \[ L_i L_j - L_j L_i = \sum_{k=1}^r c^k_{ij}(x) L_k . \]
nodes.statement_short: Linearly independent first-order operators $L_i$ are in involution if their commutators are combinations of the $L_k$.
nodes.label: def:invol

nodes.name: local Frobenius theorem
nodes.statement: If the first order differential operators $L_i$, $i=1,\ldots,r \le m$, are in involution, then there exist $m-r$ smooth functions $u^k(x)$ that satisfy the equations $L_i u^k(x) = 0$ and such that their gradients $\nabla u^k(x)$, $k=1,\ldots,m-r$ are linearly independent.
assumptions: the first order differential operators $L_i$, $i=1,\ldots,r \le m$, are in involution
conclusions: there exist $m-r$ smooth functions $u^k(x)$ that satisfy the equations $L_i u^k(x) = 0$ and such that their gradients $\nabla u^k(x)$, $k=1,\ldots,m-r$ are linearly independent
nodes.statement_short: An involutive system of $r$ first-order operators has $m-r$ functionally independent common solutions $L_i u = 0$.
nodes.label: thm:frob-loc

nodes.name: proof of the local Frobenius theorem
nodes.statement: This proof consists of chaining together several intermediate results, which are proven in separate lemmas below. The first step is to replace the $L_i$ operators by some better behaved operators $L'_{i'}$, namely satisfying $[L'_{i'}, L'_{j'}] = 0$ (Lem.~\ref{lem:loc-init-split}(e)) and having a form adapted to a split local coordinate system $(y,z)$ around $x_0$. The equations $L'_{i'} u = 0$ and $L_i u = 0$ are equivalent (Lem.~\ref{lem:op-frame}, \ref{lem:eq-frame-equiv}). Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-radial} shows that there exists a new local coordinate system $(y,\bar{Z})$ on a neighborhood of $x_0$, where $\bar{Z}^k=\bar{Z}^k(y,z)$, which is better adapted to our differential equations. Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-loc-inv} actually shows that the contructed coordinates give us the desired solutions via $u^k(x) = \bar{Z}^k(y(x),z(x))$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain the lemmas: straighten the operators to commuting form in split coordinates, then build the solution coordinates via the radial ODE.

nodes.name: Proof is a chain of the lemmas below
nodes.statement: This proof consists of chaining together several intermediate results, which are proven in separate lemmas below.
nodes.statement_short: Proof is a chain of the lemmas below

nodes.name: Replace $L_i$ by commuting operators $L'_{i'}$ adapted to split coordinates
nodes.statement: The first step is to replace the $L_i$ operators by some better behaved operators $L'_{i'}$, namely satisfying $[L'_{i'}, L'_{j'}] = 0$ (Lem.~\ref{lem:loc-init-split}(e)) and having a form adapted to a split local coordinate system $(y,z)$ around $x_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $L_i$ by commuting operators $L'_{i'}$ adapted to split coordinates

nodes.name: Equations for $L$ and $L'$ are equivalent
nodes.statement: The equations $L'_{i'} u = 0$ and $L_i u = 0$ are equivalent (Lem.~\ref{lem:op-frame}, \ref{lem:eq-frame-equiv}).
nodes.statement_short: Equations for $L$ and $L'$ are equivalent

nodes.name: Construct adapted coordinates $(y,\bar Z)$
nodes.statement: Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-radial} shows that there exists a new local coordinate system $(y,\bar{Z})$ on a neighborhood of $x_0$, where $\bar{Z}^k=\bar{Z}^k(y,z)$, which is better adapted to our differential equations.
nodes.statement_short: Construct adapted coordinates $(y,\bar Z)$

nodes.name: The $\bar Z^k$ give the desired solutions
nodes.statement: Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-loc-inv} actually shows that the contructed coordinates give us the desired solutions via $u^k(x) = \bar{Z}^k(y(x),z(x))$.
nodes.statement_short: The $\bar Z^k$ give the desired solutions

nodes.name: change of frame preserves involution
nodes.statement: If the $L_i$ as in Def.~\ref{def:invol} are in infolution, then the $L'_{i'} = \sum_{i=1}^r \alpha_{i'}^i L_i$, $i'=1,\ldots,r$, with smooth pointwise invertible $\alpha_{i'}^i$, are also in involution.
assumptions: the $L_i$ as in Def.~\ref{def:invol} are in infolution
conclusions: the $L'_{i'} = \sum_{i=1}^r \alpha_{i'}^i L_i$, $i'=1,\ldots,r$, with smooth pointwise invertible $\alpha_{i'}^i$, are also in involution
nodes.statement_short: Involutivity is preserved under an invertible smooth change of frame $L' = \alpha L$.
nodes.label: lem:op-frame

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: It is sufficient to compute the commutator \begin{align*} L'_{i'} L'_{j'} - L'_{j'} L'_{i'} &= \alpha_{i'}^i \alpha_{j'}^j (L_i L_j - L_j L_i) + \alpha_{i'}^i L_i(\alpha_{j'}^j) L_j - \alpha_{j'}^j L_j(\alpha_{i'}^i) L_i \\ &= \alpha_{i'}^i \alpha_{j'}^j \left(c_{ij}^k + (\alpha^{-1})_j^{j'} L_i(\alpha_{j'}^j) \delta_j^k - (\alpha^{-1})_i^{i'} L_j(\alpha_{i'}^i) \delta_i^k \right) L_k \\ &= \alpha_{i'}^i \alpha_{j'}^j \left(c_{ij}^k + (\alpha^{-1})_j^{j'} L_i(\alpha_{j'}^j) \delta_j^k - (\alpha^{-1})_i^{i'} L_j(\alpha_{i'}^i) \delta_i^k \right) (\alpha^{-1})_k^{k'} L'_{k'} \\ &= \sum_{k'=1}^r c'^{k'}_{i'j'} L'_{k'} , \end{align*} where the formula for $c'^{k'}_{i'j'}$ can be read off from the last equality.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the commutator of $L'$ via the Leibniz rule and re-express in the $L'$ frame.

nodes.name: equivalence of equations under change of frame
nodes.statement: For the operators $L'_{i'}$ as in Lem.~\ref{lem:op-frame}, a smooth function $u$ solves $L_i u = 0$, $i=1,\ldots,r$, iff it solves $L'_{i'} u = 0$, $i'=1,\ldots,r$.
conclusions: a smooth function $u$ solves $L_i u = 0$, $i=1,\ldots,r$, iff it solves $L'_{i'} u = 0$, $i'=1,\ldots,r$
nodes.label: lem:eq-frame-equiv

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: The computation \[ L'_{i'} u = \sum_{i=1}^r \alpha_{i'}^i (L_i u) \] shows that $L_i u = 0$, $i=1,\ldots,r$, implies $L'_{i'} u = 0$ for any $i'=1,\ldots,r$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation $L' u = \alpha (L u)$ (one direction shown).

nodes.name: local straightening to split commuting frame
nodes.statement: For the operators $L_i$ from Def.~\ref{def:invol}, given $x_0 \in M$, there exists an open coordinate neighborhood $U\ni x_0$ such that (a) there an exists invertible $\alpha_{i'}^i$ as in Lem.~\ref{lem:op-frame}, (b) there exists a split local chart $(y,z)\colon M \supset U' \cong \mathbb{R}^r \times \mathbb{R}^{m-r}$, with (c) $(y(x_0),z(x_0)) = (0,0)$, (d) \[ L'_{i'} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} + \sum_{j=1}^{m-r} f_{i'}^j(y,z) \frac{\partial}{\partial z^j} . \] and (e) $[L'_{i'}, L'_{j'}] = 0$, for $i',j'=1,\ldots,r$, which expressed in terms of $f_{i'}^j$ means (f) \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} f_{j'}^j + \sum_{k=1}^{m-r} f_{i'}^k \frac{\partial}{\partial z^k} f_{j'}^j = \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{j'}} f_{i'}^j + \sum_{k=1}^{m-r} f_{j'}^k \frac{\partial}{\partial z^k} f_{i'}^j . \]
conclusions: there exists an open coordinate neighborhood $U\ni x_0$ such that
nodes.statement_short: Near $x_0$ there are split coordinates $(y,z)$ and a frame change making $L'_{i'} = \partial_{y^{i'}} + f_{i'}^j\partial_{z^j}$ commute.
nodes.label: lem:loc-init-split

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: Start with the coordinates $(x^1,\ldots,x^m)$ on $U$ and consider the coordinate components $L_i = a_i^j(x) \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}$. The rank of the matrix $a_i^j(x_0)$ must be $r$, otherwise the $L_i$ vectors do not constitute a frame for the distribution $\mathcal{D}$. Hence, there exists a subset $I \subseteq \{1,\ldots,r\}$ such that the matrix minor $(a_i^j)_{i\in I, 1\le j\le m}$ is non-singular. Define the coordinates $y^{i'} = x^{I(i')} - (x_0)^{I(i')}$, $i'=1,\ldots,r$, and $z^{j} = x^{I^c(j)} - (x_0)^{I^c(j)}$, $j=1,\ldots,m-r$, where $I(i')$ and $I^c(j)$ is some ordering of the sets $I$ and its complement $I^c$. Then, restrict to a sub-neighborhood $U'' \subseteq U$ that is split with respect to the $(y,z)$ coordinates. The new coordinate components are \[ L_{i} = \sum_{i'=1}^r a_{i}^{I(i')}(x(y,z)) \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} + \sum_{j=1}^{m-r} a_{i}^{I^c(j)}(x(y,z)) \frac{\partial}{\partial z^j} . \] Let $\beta_{i}^{i'}(y,z) = a_{i}^{I(i')}(x(y,z))$ and $\gamma_{i}^{j}(y,z) = a_{i}^{I^c(j)}(x(y,z))$, so that by construction $\beta_{i}^{i'}(0,0)$ is non-singular. Since $\beta \colon U'' \to \operatorname{Mat}(r,r)$ is smooth (hence a fortiriori continuous) and the subset of non-singular matrices in $\operatorname{Mat}(r,r)$ is open, there is a possibly smaller split sub-neighborhood $U' \subseteq U''$ on which $\beta$ is everywhere non-singular. So, defining $\alpha_{i'}^j(y,z) = (\beta_{i}^{i'}(y,z))^{-1}$ on $U''$ satisfies the desired conclusions (a), (b), (c) and (d), where $f_{i'}^j(y,z) = \alpha_{i'}^i(y,z) \gamma_{i}^j(y,z)$. To prove (e) and (f), consider the computation \begin{align*} [L'_{i'}, L'_{j'}] &= L'_{i'} L'_{j'} - L'_{j'} L'_{i'} \\ = \sum_{k'=1}^r c'^{k'}_{i'j'} L'_{k'} &= \sum_{j=1}^{m-r} \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} f_{j'}^j - \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{j'}} f_{i'}^j\right)\frac{\partial}{\partial z^j} + \sum_{k=1}^{m-r} \sum_{j=1}^{m-r} \left(f_{i'}^j \frac{\partial}{\partial z^j} f_{j'}^k - f_{j'}^j \frac{\partial}{\partial z^j} f_{i'}^k\right) \frac{\partial}{\partial z^k} \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^{m-r} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} f_{j'}^j + \sum_{k=1}^{m-r} f_{i'}^k \frac{\partial}{\partial z^k} f_{j'}^j - \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{j'}} f_{i'}^j - \sum_{k=1}^{m-r} f_{j'}^k \frac{\partial}{\partial z^k} f_{i'}^j . \right) \end{align*} Hence, for each fixed $i',j'$, the $\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{k'}}$ components of the right-hand side vanish, while those of the left-hand side equal $\sum_{k'=1}^{m-r} c'^{k'}_{i'j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{k'}}$, meaning that all components of $c'^{k'}_{i'j'}$ must vanish, proving (e). On the other hand, the vanishing of the right-hand side of the last equality proves (f).
nodes.statement_short: Pick a non-singular minor to split coordinates, invert the $\beta$ block to normalize the frame. Commutator computation then forces $c'=0$ and yields (f).

nodes.name: inverse coordinates solve the equations
nodes.statement: Consider the operators $L'_{i'}$ and the split neighborhood $U\ni x_0$ as in Lem.~\ref{lem:loc-init-split}. Let $Z^k(y,z)$ and $\bar{Z}^k(y,z)$ satisfy the inversion identity $\bar{Z}^k(y, Z(y, z)) = z^k$, for all $z$ on a sufficiently small neighborhood of $z=0$, and for all $y$ on a sufficiently small neighborhood of $y=0$. Suppose that $Z^j(y,z)$ satisfies (a) $Z^j(0,z) = z^j$ and (b) \[ \frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial y^{i'}}(y,z) = f_{i'}^j(y, Z^j(y,z)) . \] Then \[ L'_{i'} \bar{Z}(y,z) = 0, \quad i'=1,\ldots,r , \] and vice versa.
assumptions: Consider the operators $L'_{i'}$ and the split neighborhood $U\ni x_0$ as in Lem.~\ref{lem:loc-init-split}.

Let $Z^k(y,z)$ and $\bar{Z}^k(y,z)$ satisfy the inversion identity $\bar{Z}^k(y, Z(y, z)) = z^k$, for all $z$ on a sufficiently small neighborhood of $z=0$, and for all $y$ on a sufficiently small neighborhood of $y=0$.
nodes.statement_short: If $Z$ solves $\partial_y Z = f(y,Z)$ with $Z(0,z)=z$, its inverse $\bar Z$ is annihilated by all $L'_{i'}$, and conversely.
nodes.label: lem:eq-loc-inv

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: Start by differentiating the inversion identity: \begin{align*} 0 = \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} z^k &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \bar{Z}^k(y, Z(y, z)) \\ &= \left. \frac{\partial \bar{Z}^k}{\partial y^{i'}}(y, z') \right|_{z'=Z(y,z)} + \frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial y^{i'}}(y,z) \left. \frac{\partial \bar{Z}^k}{\partial z'^j}(y,z') \right|_{z'=Z(y,z)} \\ &= \left. \left(\frac{\partial \bar{Z}^k}{\partial y^{i'}}(y, z') + f_{i'}^j(y,z') \frac{\partial \bar{Z}^k}{\partial z'^j}(y,z')\right) \right|_{z'=Z(y,z)} \\ &\quad {} + \left. \left(\frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial y^{i'}}(y,z) - f_{i'}^j(y,z')\right) \frac{\partial \bar{Z}^k}{\partial z'^j}(y,z') \right|_{z'=Z(y,z)} . \end{align*} Recall that being a diffeomorphism, the Jacobian $\frac{\partial \bar{Z}^k}{\partial z'^j}(y,z')$ non-singular on the sufficiently small split domain, with $(\frac{\partial \bar{Z}^k}{\partial z'^j}(y,z'))^{-1} = \left. \frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial z^k}(y,z) \right|_{z=\bar{Z}(y,z')}$. Hence, rearranging the last equality, we find \[ \left. \frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial z^k}(y,z) L'_{i'} \bar{Z}^k(y,z') \right|_{z'=Z(y,z)} = -\left(\frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial y^{i'}}(y,z) - f_{i'}^j(y,Z(y,z))\right) . \] Hence, if one side of the equality vanishes, then so does the other, which proves the desired equivalence.
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the inversion identity by the chain rule and use invertibility of the Jacobian of $\bar Z$.

nodes.name: Differentiate the inversion identity
nodes.statement: Start by differentiating the inversion identity: \begin{align*} 0 = \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} z^k &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \bar{Z}^k(y, Z(y, z)) \\ &= \left. \frac{\partial \bar{Z}^k}{\partial y^{i'}}(y, z') \right|_{z'=Z(y,z)} + \frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial y^{i'}}(y,z) \left. \frac{\partial \bar{Z}^k}{\partial z'^j}(y,z') \right|_{z'=Z(y,z)} \\ &= \left. \left(\frac{\partial \bar{Z}^k}{\partial y^{i'}}(y, z') + f_{i'}^j(y,z') \frac{\partial \bar{Z}^k}{\partial z'^j}(y,z')\right) \right|_{z'=Z(y,z)} \\ &\quad {} + \left. \left(\frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial y^{i'}}(y,z) - f_{i'}^j(y,z')\right) \frac{\partial \bar{Z}^k}{\partial z'^j}(y,z') \right|_{z'=Z(y,z)} . \end{align*}

nodes.name: radial ODE reformulation
nodes.statement: Let $Z^j(y,z)$ be as in Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-loc-inv}. Then, $\zeta^j(t,y,z) = Z^j(ty,z)$ satisfies $\zeta^j(0,y,z) = z^j$ and the equations \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \zeta^j(t,y,z) = y^{i'} f_{i'}^j(ty,\zeta(t,y,z)) . \] Conversely, if $\zeta^j(t,y,z)$ satisfies the initial value problem above, then there exists a sufficiently small neighborhood of $(y,z)=(0,0)$ for which $Z^j(ty,z)$ exists up to at least $t=1$. Then $Z^j(y,z) = \zeta^j(1,y,z)$ satisfies the conditions in the hypotheses of Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-loc-inv}.

nodes.statement_short: The PDE system for $Z$ is equivalent to the radial ODE for $\zeta(t,y,z)=Z(ty,z)$, solved up to $t=1$.
nodes.label: lem:eq-radial

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: The easy direction is proved by the following computation: \begin{align*} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \zeta^j(t,y,z) &= \frac{\partial}{\partial t} Z^j(ty,z) \\ &= y^{i'} \left.\frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial y'^{i'}}(y',z) \right|_{y'=ty} \\ &= y^{i'} \left.f_{i'}^j(y',Z^j(y',z)) \right|_{y'=ty} \\ &= y^{i'} f_{i'}^j(ty,Z(ty,z)) = y^{i'} f_{i'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z)) . \end{align*} For the converse direction, consider the following computation, where we use the ODE satisfied by $\zeta^j(t,y,z)$ and the identity from Lem.~\ref{lem:loc-init-split}(f): \begin{align*} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^j(t,y,z) - t f_{i'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z))\right) &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \zeta^j(t,y,z) \\ &\quad{} - f_{i'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z)) - \left.t y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial y'^{j'}} f_{i'}^{j}(y', \zeta(t,y,z))\right|_{y'=ty} - t \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \zeta^k(t,y,z)\right) \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{i'}^j(ty, z')\right|_{z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \\ &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \left(y^{j'} f_{j'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z))\right) \\ &\quad{} - f_{i'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z)) - t y^{j'} \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial y'^{j'}} f_{i'}^{j}(y', z')\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} - t y^{j'} \left. f_{j'}^k(y',z') \frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{i'}^j(y', z')\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \\ &= \left.\left(f_{i'}^{j}(y', z') + t y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial y'^{i'}} f_{j'}^j(y', z') + \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^k(t,y,z)\right) y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{j'}^j(y', z') \right)\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \\ &\quad{} - \left.\left( f_{i'}^j(y', z') + t y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial y'^{i'}} f_{j'}^{j}(y', z') + t y^{j'} f_{i'}^k(y',z') \frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{j'}^j(y', z') \right)\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \\ &= \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^k(t,y,z) - t f_{i'}^k(ty, \zeta(t,y,z))\right) \left. y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{j'}^j(y', z')\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \end{align*} Hence, we find that $\eta(t,y,z) = \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^k(t,y,z) - t f_{i'}^k(ty, \zeta(t,y,z))$ satisfies a linear ODE. Hence, by the uniqueness of ODE solutions (Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-radial-exists}(b)), if the initial condition $\eta(0,y,z) = 0$ is satisfied, the solution must identically vanish, $\eta(t,y,z) = 0$, which upon setting $t=1$ proves that $Z^j(y,z) = \zeta^j(1,y,z)$ satisfies the desired differential equation, (Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-radial-exists}(c)). It remains to check the vanishing initial condition: \begin{align*} \eta(0,y,z) &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^j(0,y,z) - 0 \cdot f_{i'}^j(0 \zeta(0,y,z)) \\ &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} z^j - 0 = 0 . \end{align*} The proof is completed by noting that the inverse function $\bar{Z}(y,z)$ exists on a sufficiently small neighborhood of $(y,z)=(0,0)$, because the continuity of $\frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial z^k}$ and the property that $\left.\frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial_z^k}\right|_{z=0} = \delta^j_k$ ensures that $Z^j(y,z)$ is an immersion (has non-singular jacobian) on a neighborhood of $(y,z)=(0,0)$ and hence a diffeomorphism on a possibly smaller neighborhood (use inverse function theorem).
nodes.statement_short: Easy direction by chain rule. Converse: the defect $\eta$ satisfies a linear ODE with zero initial data, so vanishes by ODE uniqueness; invert $Z$ by the inverse function theorem.

nodes.name: Easy direction by computation
nodes.statement: The easy direction is proved by the following computation: \begin{align*} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \zeta^j(t,y,z) &= \frac{\partial}{\partial t} Z^j(ty,z) \\ &= y^{i'} \left.\frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial y'^{i'}}(y',z) \right|_{y'=ty} \\ &= y^{i'} \left.f_{i'}^j(y',Z^j(y',z)) \right|_{y'=ty} \\ &= y^{i'} f_{i'}^j(ty,Z(ty,z)) = y^{i'} f_{i'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z)) . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Easy direction: chain rule computation

nodes.name: Converse direction
nodes.statement: For the converse direction, consider the following computation, where we use the ODE satisfied by $\zeta^j(t,y,z)$ and the identity from Lem.~\ref{lem:loc-init-split}(f): \begin{align*} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^j(t,y,z) - t f_{i'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z))\right) &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \zeta^j(t,y,z) \\ &\quad{} - f_{i'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z)) - \left.t y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial y'^{j'}} f_{i'}^{j}(y', \zeta(t,y,z))\right|_{y'=ty} - t \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \zeta^k(t,y,z)\right) \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{i'}^j(ty, z')\right|_{z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \\ &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \left(y^{j'} f_{j'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z))\right) \\ &\quad{} - f_{i'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z)) - t y^{j'} \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial y'^{j'}} f_{i'}^{j}(y', z')\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} - t y^{j'} \left. f_{j'}^k(y',z') \frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{i'}^j(y', z')\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \\ &= \left.\left(f_{i'}^{j}(y', z') + t y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial y'^{i'}} f_{j'}^j(y', z') + \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^k(t,y,z)\right) y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{j'}^j(y', z') \right)\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \\ &\quad{} - \left.\left( f_{i'}^j(y', z') + t y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial y'^{i'}} f_{j'}^{j}(y', z') + t y^{j'} f_{i'}^k(y',z') \frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{j'}^j(y', z') \right)\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \\ &= \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^k(t,y,z) - t f_{i'}^k(ty, \zeta(t,y,z))\right) \left. y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{j'}^j(y', z')\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \end{align*} Hence, we find that $\eta(t,y,z) = \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^k(t,y,z) - t f_{i'}^k(ty, \zeta(t,y,z))$ satisfies a linear ODE. Hence, by the uniqueness of ODE solutions (Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-radial-exists}(b)), if the initial condition $\eta(0,y,z) = 0$ is satisfied, the solution must identically vanish, $\eta(t,y,z) = 0$, which upon setting $t=1$ proves that $Z^j(y,z) = \zeta^j(1,y,z)$ satisfies the desired differential equation, (Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-radial-exists}(c)). It remains to check the vanishing initial condition: \begin{align*} \eta(0,y,z) &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^j(0,y,z) - 0 \cdot f_{i'}^j(0 \zeta(0,y,z)) \\ &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} z^j - 0 = 0 . \end{align*} The proof is completed by noting that the inverse function $\bar{Z}(y,z)$ exists on a sufficiently small neighborhood of $(y,z)=(0,0)$, because the continuity of $\frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial z^k}$ and the property that $\left.\frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial_z^k}\right|_{z=0} = \delta^j_k$ ensures that $Z^j(y,z)$ is an immersion (has non-singular jacobian) on a neighborhood of $(y,z)=(0,0)$ and hence a diffeomorphism on a possibly smaller neighborhood (use inverse function theorem).
nodes.statement_short: Converse: show the defect $\eta$ vanishes

nodes.name: Differentiate the defect using the ODE and Lemma 3(f)
nodes.statement: For the converse direction, consider the following computation, where we use the ODE satisfied by $\zeta^j(t,y,z)$ and the identity from Lem.~\ref{lem:loc-init-split}(f): \begin{align*} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^j(t,y,z) - t f_{i'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z))\right) &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \zeta^j(t,y,z) \\ &\quad{} - f_{i'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z)) - \left.t y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial y'^{j'}} f_{i'}^{j}(y', \zeta(t,y,z))\right|_{y'=ty} - t \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \zeta^k(t,y,z)\right) \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{i'}^j(ty, z')\right|_{z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \\ &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \left(y^{j'} f_{j'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z))\right) \\ &\quad{} - f_{i'}^j(ty, \zeta(t,y,z)) - t y^{j'} \left. \frac{\partial}{\partial y'^{j'}} f_{i'}^{j}(y', z')\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} - t y^{j'} \left. f_{j'}^k(y',z') \frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{i'}^j(y', z')\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \\ &= \left.\left(f_{i'}^{j}(y', z') + t y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial y'^{i'}} f_{j'}^j(y', z') + \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^k(t,y,z)\right) y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{j'}^j(y', z') \right)\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \\ &\quad{} - \left.\left( f_{i'}^j(y', z') + t y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial y'^{i'}} f_{j'}^{j}(y', z') + t y^{j'} f_{i'}^k(y',z') \frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{j'}^j(y', z') \right)\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \\ &= \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^k(t,y,z) - t f_{i'}^k(ty, \zeta(t,y,z))\right) \left. y^{j'} \frac{\partial}{\partial z'^k} f_{j'}^j(y', z')\right|_{y'=ty, z'=\zeta(t,y,z)} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the defect using the ODE and Lemma 3(f)

nodes.name: Defect $\eta$ satisfies a linear ODE
nodes.statement: Hence, we find that $\eta(t,y,z) = \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^k(t,y,z) - t f_{i'}^k(ty, \zeta(t,y,z))$ satisfies a linear ODE.
nodes.statement_short: Defect $\eta$ satisfies a linear ODE

nodes.name: ODE uniqueness gives $\eta\equiv0$
nodes.statement: Hence, by the uniqueness of ODE solutions (Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-radial-exists}(b)), if the initial condition $\eta(0,y,z) = 0$ is satisfied, the solution must identically vanish, $\eta(t,y,z) = 0$, which upon setting $t=1$ proves that $Z^j(y,z) = \zeta^j(1,y,z)$ satisfies the desired differential equation, (Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-radial-exists}(c)).
nodes.statement_short: ODE uniqueness gives $\eta\equiv0$

nodes.name: Check $\eta(0,y,z)=0$
nodes.statement: It remains to check the vanishing initial condition: \begin{align*} \eta(0,y,z) &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} \zeta^j(0,y,z) - 0 \cdot f_{i'}^j(0 \zeta(0,y,z)) \\ &= \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{i'}} z^j - 0 = 0 . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Check $\eta(0,y,z)=0$

nodes.name: Invert $Z$ via the inverse function theorem
nodes.statement: The proof is completed by noting that the inverse function $\bar{Z}(y,z)$ exists on a sufficiently small neighborhood of $(y,z)=(0,0)$, because the continuity of $\frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial z^k}$ and the property that $\left.\frac{\partial Z^j}{\partial_z^k}\right|_{z=0} = \delta^j_k$ ensures that $Z^j(y,z)$ is an immersion (has non-singular jacobian) on a neighborhood of $(y,z)=(0,0)$ and hence a diffeomorphism on a possibly smaller neighborhood (use inverse function theorem).
nodes.statement_short: Invert $Z$ via the inverse function theorem

nodes.name: ODE existence, uniqueness and smooth dependence
nodes.statement: An ODE initial value problem (a sufficiently general one to cover the one for $\zeta^j(t,y,z)$ in Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-radial} and the one for $\eta_{i'}^j(t,y,z)$ in the proof of Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-radial}) (a) has a solution that is jointly smooth in $(t,y,z)$, which (b) is unique, and (c) exists (at least) up to time $t=1$ on a sufficiently small neighborhood of $(y,z) = (0,0)$.
assumptions: An ODE initial value problem (a sufficiently general one to cover the one for $\zeta^j(t,y,z)$ in Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-radial} and the one for $\eta_{i'}^j(t,y,z)$ in the proof of Lem.~\ref{lem:eq-radial})
conclusions: (a) has a solution that is jointly smooth in $(t,y,z)$
(c) exists (at least) up to time $t=1$ on a sufficiently small neighborhood of $(y,z) = (0,0)$
nodes.statement_short: The relevant ODE IVPs have unique jointly smooth solutions existing up to $t=1$ near the origin.
nodes.label: lem:eq-radial-exists

nodes.name: proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement: This should follow from the Picard-Lindel\"of ODE existence and uniqueness theorem with parameters.
nodes.statement_short: Appeal to the Picard-Lindelof theorem with parameters.

nodes.name: differential form Frobenius theorem
nodes.statement: If $\alpha_i$, $i=1,\ldots k\le m-k$ are 1-forms on $M$ that generate a closed differential ideal. Then there exist smooth scalar functions $u_i(x)$, $i=1,\ldots,m-k$ such that the exact 1-forms $du_i$, $i=1,\ldots,m-k$ generate the same differential ideal.
assumptions: $\alpha_i$, $i=1,\ldots k\le m-k$ are 1-forms on $M$ that generate a closed differential ideal
conclusions: there exist smooth scalar functions $u_i(x)$, $i=1,\ldots,m-k$ such that the exact 1-forms $du_i$, $i=1,\ldots,m-k$ generate the same differential ideal
nodes.statement_short: A closed differential ideal generated by 1-forms is generated by exact forms $du_i$.
nodes.label: thm:frob-forms

nodes.name: tangent distribution
nodes.statement: A \emph{tangent distribution} on a manifold $M$ is a vector sub-bundle $\mathcal{D}\hookrightarrow TM$ (equivalently, an embedding of vector bundles).
nodes.label: def:vec-dist

nodes.name: Lie bracket
nodes.statement: On a manifold $M$, given two vector fields $u$, $v$ (sections of the tangent bundle $TM$), their \emph{Lie bracket} $w = [u,v]$ is the vector field that satisfies the identity $w(f) = u(v(f)) - v(u(f))$, where vector fields act as first order differential operators on a smooth function $f$. In coordinate form, if $u = u^i\partial_i$, $v = v^i\partial_i$, $w = w^i\partial_i$, then $w^j = u^i \partial_i v^j - v^i \partial_i u^i$. The vector fields $u$, $v$ \emph{commute} (or are \emph{in involution} in the sense of Def.~\ref{def:invol}) if $[u,v] = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Lie bracket $[u,v]$ is the commutator vector field; $u,v$ commute if $[u,v]=0$.
nodes.label: def:lie

nodes.name: involutive distribution
nodes.statement: A tangent distribution $\mathcal{D} \hookrightarrow TM$ is \emph{involutive} if, for any two vector field sections $u$, $v$ of $\mathcal{D}$, the Lie bracket $[u,v]$ is also a section of $\mathcal{D}$.
differentia: for any two vector field sections $u$, $v$ of $\mathcal{D}$, the Lie bracket $[u,v]$ is also a section of $\mathcal{D}$
nodes.label: def:inv-distr

nodes.name: integral submanifold
nodes.statement: Given a manifold $M$ with a tangent distribution $\mathcal{D} \hookrightarrow TM$ of rank $r$ (as a vector bundle), a submanifold $\iota\colon N \hookrightarrow M$ passing through $x_0 \in M$ is called an \emph{integral submanifold} of the distribution $\mathcal{D}$ if it is everywhere tangent to $\mathcal{D}$, $T\iota (TN) \subseteq \mathcal{D}$, where naturally $\dim N \le r$. In the case $\dim N = r$, the integral submanifold is called \emph{maximal (in dimension)}.
nodes.statement_short: A submanifold everywhere tangent to $\mathcal{D}$; maximal when its dimension equals the rank.
nodes.label: def:int-subman

nodes.name: vector field Frobenius theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D} \subseteq TM$ be an involutive tangent space distribution of rank $r\le m = \dim M$. Then, for every $x_0\in M$, there exists a maximal integral submanifold $\iota\colon \mathbb{R}^n \hookrightarrow M$ of $\mathcal{D}$ such that $\iota(0) = x_0$. Moreover, these integral submanifolds collect into a $r$-dimensional foliation of $M$ whose leaves are everywhere tangent to the distribution $\mathcal{D}$.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{D} \subseteq TM$ be an involutive tangent space distribution of rank $r\le m = \dim M$.
conclusions: for every $x_0\in M$, there exists a maximal integral submanifold $\iota\colon \mathbb{R}^n \hookrightarrow M$ of $\mathcal{D}$ such that $\iota(0) = x_0$.
these integral submanifolds collect into a $r$-dimensional foliation of $M$ whose leaves are everywhere tangent to the distribution $\mathcal{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: An involutive distribution has maximal integral submanifolds through every point, forming a foliation.
nodes.label: thm:frob-vec
